title: Static Libraries, DLLs or Header-Only
summary: You now know what DLLs cost and what they give. This lesson compares the three ways to package reusable C++ code - header-only, static library, DLL - and gives a short set of questions for choosing, with examples from real projects.
markdown:
## The three packages

**Header-only.** All the code is in headers, often templates or `inline` functions. Every program that includes them compiles its own copy. Examples: much of the standard library, `{fmt}`, `nlohmann/json`, Dear ImGui's helpers.

**Static library (`.lib`).** Compiled once into object code; the linker copies what each program uses into its `.exe`. Examples: most libraries you get through a package manager by default.

**DLL.** Compiled once into its own file; programs load it when they start or while they run. Examples: the Windows API, graphics drivers, the C runtime, plugin systems.

## Side by side

| | Header-only | Static library | DLL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Build cost for users | Highest: recompiled in every file that includes it | Low | Low |
| Optimisation across the boundary | Full: the compiler sees everything | Good (with link-time code generation) | None: calls go through the import table |
| Templates in the interface | Yes | Only already-used types | Only through a C or COM-style interface |
| Files to ship | None | None | The DLL |
| Update without rebuilding programs | No | No | **Yes** |
| Load or unload while running | No | No | **Yes** |
| Shared between processes | No | No | **Yes**, code pages |
| Usable from other languages | No | Only from C/C++ | **Yes**, with a C interface |
| ABI concerns | None | Same compiler and settings | Must be designed for (milestone 3) |

## Questions to choose with

Ask them in order; the first "yes" usually decides.

1. **Do other languages or other teams' programs need to call it?** A DLL with a C interface.
2. **Must it be loaded, swapped or unloaded while running** (plugins, mods, hot reload)? A DLL.
3. **Must it be updated without rebuilding the programs that use it** (a driver, a shared component)? A DLL.
4. **Is it mostly templates, or small?** Header-only.
5. **Otherwise:** a static library. It is the simplest thing that works: one file to ship, no ABI to design, no search order, no loader lock.

## How real game projects use them

- **Engine as DLLs, during development only.** Engines such as Unreal build each module (`Core`, `Renderer`, `Physics`...) as a DLL in development, so editing one module relinks one small DLL instead of the whole game, and enables hot reload. Shipping builds link the same code **statically** into one executable for speed and simplicity. Both use the same source; a build setting switches the export macro to nothing.
- **Gameplay code as a DLL** while developing, reloaded on every rebuild (lesson 5.03).
- **Mods and plugins** as DLLs with a stable C or COM-style interface (lessons 5.01 and 5.02).
- **Third-party SDKs** (audio middleware, platform services) usually as DLLs, because they are updated separately from your game.

## One codebase, both ways

The export macro from lesson 1.03 can do double duty:

```cpp-norun
#if defined(STONEMATH_STATIC)
#define STONEMATH_API                              // linked statically: no import or export
#elif defined(STONEMATH_EXPORTS)
#define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllexport)
#else
#define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllimport)
#endif
```

Define `STONEMATH_STATIC` in both the library and the program when you build the library as a static `.lib`.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Making everything a DLL "for modularity"
> Modularity is about interfaces, not file formats. Every DLL adds a boundary with real rules. Use one when you need what only a DLL gives.

> [!warning] A header-only library that is huge
> Every file that includes it pays to compile it. Split heavy code into a compiled library and keep the header light.

## Knowledge check

```quiz
? A library must be callable from C# and Python. What should it be?
+ A DLL with a C interface
- A header-only library
- A static library
> Other languages can only load DLLs and call C functions.

? Which package lets the compiler optimise across the boundary the most?
+ Header-only
- DLL
- They are all the same
> The compiler sees all of the code in each program.

? Why do engines often use DLLs in development but static linking for shipping?
+ DLLs make rebuilds faster and allow hot reload; static linking ships one fast, simple executable
- Static linking is not allowed during development
- DLLs are required by consoles
> The same source is built both ways with a switch in the export macro.
```
ideas: - Add `STONEMATH_STATIC` to your StoneMath header and build it both as a DLL and as a static library, then compare the program's size and `dumpbin /dependents`.

cards.q: Name three things only a DLL can do.
cards.a: Be updated without rebuilding programs, be loaded and unloaded while running, share code pages between processes, and be called from other languages.

cards.q: When is a static library the right choice?
cards.a: When none of those are needed: it is the simplest option, with no extra files, no ABI design and no loading rules.

cards.q: How can one library be built either as a DLL or statically?
cards.a: With an export macro that expands to nothing when a STATIC symbol is defined, dllexport when building the DLL, and dllimport otherwise.
